title: One equation, three unknowns: what must be true
summary: Every development deal can be written as one equation linking land price, building income and the return a buyer needs. Public information usually reveals two of the three, so you can solve for the third. The skill is not the arithmetic; it is turning the answer into a short list of things that must be true, and testing each against evidence.
body:
Mr Shabazz, every deal is one equation with three big unknowns: what was paid for the land, what the finished building will earn, and what return the buyer needs. Public information usually hands you two of them. Reverse engineering is solving for the third and then asking, calmly, whether that answer is believable.

Recall

Q. From the valuation week: how do you turn an appraised value back into the rent it requires?

A. Multiply the value by the cap rate to get net operating income (NOI), add back operating expenses and vacancy to reach gross income, then divide by the number of apartments and by twelve months. Compare that rent with what tenants actually pay today.

Q. From the returns week: what does the equity multiple tell you that the internal rate of return (IRR) does not?

A. How much money comes back for each dollar put in. IRR measures speed; the multiple measures amount. A quick small deal can have a high IRR and a thin multiple.

Q. From the first phase: what is a go/no-go gate?

A. A fixed point in a project where you decide, against criteria written in advance, whether to commit more money. Dates, announcements and money already spent do not move you past it; only the criteria do.

Why this matters

Every day someone will tell you a number: a land price, a rent, a return. A broker, a seller, a partner, a lender, a newspaper. You cannot audit their spreadsheet, but you do not need to. If you know how the pieces of a deal fit together, you can take the one number they give you and work out what else must be true for it to make sense. That turns a sales pitch into a set of testable claims. It is the cheapest diligence you will ever do, and it happens before you spend a dollar on consultants.

The equation

Plain English first. A building is worth what it earns, divided by the yield buyers accept. It costs land plus construction plus fees plus interest. The developer's margin is the gap between the two. Everything in this week hangs on those three sentences.

The professional framing uses four terms you already know. Value equals stabilised NOI divided by the market capitalisation rate, or cap rate. Total cost equals land plus hard costs plus soft costs plus finance costs. Yield on cost equals stabilised NOI divided by total cost. The development spread is yield on cost minus the market cap rate. These are one system. Fix any three of the main inputs and the fourth is no longer a matter of opinion; it falls out of the arithmetic. That is the whole trick. The professional name for solving for the land is the residual method: land is what remains after every other claim is paid.

Worked example one: what return did the buyer accept?

Hypothetical round numbers. The land registry shows that a site sold for $3,000,000. The zoning by-law, which is public, permits 60 apartments. Listings for similar new buildings nearby ask about $2,500 a month. A published construction cost guide suggests about $200,000 per apartment in hard costs.

Build the income. Sixty apartments at $2,500 a month is $1,800,000 a year of gross rent. Assume vacancy and operating expenses take 35 percent, a common working figure for a new building but only an assumption. NOI is $1,170,000.

Build the cost. Hard costs are 60 times $200,000, which is $12,000,000. Soft costs, at a working 20 percent of hard costs, are $2,400,000. Finance costs, at 10 percent of hard costs, are $1,200,000. That is $15,600,000 before land. Add the $3,000,000 land price and total cost is $18,600,000.

Yield on cost is $1,170,000 divided by $18,600,000, about 6.3 percent. If recent sales of finished buildings show a 5 percent cap rate, the finished value is $1,170,000 divided by 0.05, which is $23,400,000. The implied profit is $4,800,000, about 26 percent on cost. You have just read the buyer's business plan without seeing it. The price looks sane on today's rents and today's costs.

Say that out loud now.

Worked example two: what can the land carry?

Now turn it around. Suppose you would need a yield on cost of 6.5 percent to take the risk, because you know lenders and investors in your market want at least about 150 basis points of spread over the cap rate. That margin is a commercial practice, not a standard; set your own and write it down.

Total cost allowed is NOI divided by your required yield: $1,170,000 divided by 0.065, which is $18,000,000. Subtract the $15,600,000 of non-land costs. The land can carry $2,400,000. The market paid $3,000,000. Either the buyer accepted a thinner margin than you would, or the buyer believes something you do not.

So ask the second question: what must be true for the $3,000,000 price to deliver your 6.5 percent? Total cost is $18,600,000, so you need NOI of 6.5 percent of that, which is $1,209,000. At a 35 percent expense load that needs gross rent of about $1,860,000, or about $2,583 a month per apartment. That is roughly 3 percent above current listings. A gap of 3 percent is a judgement call. A gap of 30 percent would be a story.

Turning the answer into a list

The output of reverse engineering is not one number. It is a short list headed "What must be true." For the example above: rents of about $2,583 a month; hard costs at or below $200,000 per apartment; the full 60 apartments approved; lease-up fast enough that finance costs stay near 10 percent of hard costs; and a 5 percent cap rate when the building is finished.

Then grade every line by the quality of its evidence. A recorded sale price on title is a fact. A permitted density in a by-law is a fact about today's rules. An asking rent is an opinion published by a landlord. A cost guide is an average that may not fit this site. A cap rate is an inference from a handful of sales. The line with the weakest evidence and the biggest effect on the answer is where your diligence money should go first.

How the best do it

Large institutional investors typically keep a record of every comparable transaction in their markets and run each one backward through the same standard model, so they can see the implied cap rate, implied land price per buildable unit and implied rent behind every reported deal. Over years that becomes a database of what the market actually accepted, rather than what brokers said it would accept. A small developer can copy this with one spreadsheet: every local land sale and building sale you hear about, with its source, its date, and the three implied numbers worked out by you. After fifty entries, you will read a new asking price in seconds.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is false precision. Every input to a reverse calculation is an estimate, and solving the equation to the nearest dollar makes an estimate look like a measurement. The control is to run every reverse calculation as a range: a low, middle and high case for each weak input, and an answer stated as a band, such as "the land carries between $2,000,000 and $2,800,000." Label the source and grade of every input in the same sheet, so anyone reading it can see which number is a fact and which is a guess.

The beginner's mistake

Assuming the other buyer was right, or assuming they were a fool. A price you cannot explain is information. Sometimes it means the buyer knows something you do not: a rezoning in progress, a tenant already signed, a cheaper way to build. Sometimes it means they overpaid. Your job is to find out which before you copy them or dismiss them. Write the question down and go looking for the answer.

Callback

In the value week, Sage taught the development spread: yield on cost minus the market cap rate, the margin you are paid for taking development risk. This week runs that same idea backward. Instead of building up to a spread from your own inputs, you start from someone else's price and ask what spread they must have accepted. If the implied spread is thin, the deal is either a bargain hidden from you or a risk nobody is being paid for.

Recap

One equation links land, cost, income and return. Public information usually reveals two or three of the pieces, so you can solve for the rest. Turn the answer into a list headed "What must be true," grade each line by its evidence, state the answer as a range, and spend your diligence money on the weakest important line.

Next: Ford, with Roman, on a public filing that let outsiders reverse engineer a famous valuation and find it did not hold.
checklist: Write the deal as one equation: value, total cost, NOI and yield on cost.
Collect the public inputs first: recorded sale price, permitted density, asking rents, cost guides.
Solve for the missing number, then write the list headed What must be true.
Grade every input as fact, rule, published opinion, average or inference.
State every reverse answer as a low, middle and high range.
Put your diligence money on the weakest input with the biggest effect.
Log each local sale with its implied cap rate, land price per unit and rent.
head: Field checklist
speak: Every deal is one equation. Value is stabilised net operating income divided by the market cap rate. Total cost is land plus hard, soft and finance costs. Yield on cost is NOI divided by total cost, and the spread is yield on cost minus the cap rate. Fix three inputs and the fourth falls out of the arithmetic. So when someone hands me a price, I solve for what they must believe. If a site sold for three million and the rents, costs and density are public, I can work out the yield on cost the buyer accepted, or the rent they need. Then I write a short list headed what must be true, and I grade each line by its evidence: a recorded sale is a fact, an asking rent is an opinion, a cap rate is an inference. I state the answer as a range, not a single figure, and I spend my diligence money on the weakest line that moves the answer most.
terms: Residual method — valuing land as whatever remains of finished value after every cost and the required profit are subtracted.
Implied assumption — a number that must be true for a stated price or return to make sense, worked out backward from the price.
Unit of comparison — a common measure such as price per buildable apartment that lets different deals be compared directly.

hostile.q: You say the land is worth 2.4 million, but the market just paid 3 million for the site next door. Why should I believe your spreadsheet over an actual sale?
hostile.a: I do not ask you to choose one. The 3 million sale is a fact, and I have reversed it: at today's listed rents and published costs it implies about a 6.3 percent yield on cost, below the margin our lenders require. For 3 million to give us 6.5 percent, rents must be about 3 percent above current listings. That is the one assumption I am testing now with a rent survey. If the survey supports it, I will raise my offer; if not, the neighbour accepted a thinner margin than we can.

role: Failure forensics (with Roman, risk and the lender's view)
title: WeWork 2019: the filing that let outsiders do the arithmetic
summary: In 2019 WeWork's public offering document gave outsiders the numbers behind a very large private valuation, and they reverse engineered it within weeks. The valuation rested on long leases funded by short memberships and on governance that favoured the founder. The lesson is to reverse every price into what it requires before you pay it.
rule: Rule 17: Before I pay or accept any price, I reverse it into the rent, occupancy, cost and return it requires, and I test each against evidence; if the public numbers cannot make the price work, I do not pay for the story.
body:
Mr Shabazz, a price can survive for years in private and collapse in weeks once outsiders can do the arithmetic. WeWork in 2019 is the clearest recent example. Roman sits beside me today, because the deepest flaw was a mismatch a lender would have spotted on the first page.

Recall

Q. From yesterday: what is the output of reverse engineering a deal?

A. A short list headed "What must be true," each line graded by the quality of its evidence. The answer is a range, not a single number.

Q. From the returns week: what is an IRR trap?

A. A way the internal rate of return misleads, for example by ranking a small quick deal above a larger one that creates more wealth, or by assuming interim cash is reinvested at the same high rate. Read it beside the equity multiple.

Q. From the first phase: what is the outside view?

A. Judging a plan by how similar plans have actually turned out, the reference class, before trusting your own detailed forecast.

Why this matters

WeWork leased office buildings and sublet desks and rooms to members. In other words it was, underneath the branding, a real estate business with a funding mismatch. Every developer who signs a long obligation against short income is running a small version of the same bet. The facts below come from public reporting and the company's own filings; verify the specifics against primary sources before you cite them in a meeting.

Step 1: Timeline

WeWork grew quickly through the 2010s, funded largely by private investors, with SoftBank the largest. A private funding round in January 2019 was widely reported to value the company at about $47 billion. In August 2019 the company, then renamed The We Company, publicly filed its registration statement for an initial public offering. In September 2019 the offering was postponed, the founder stepped down as chief executive, and the filing was later withdrawn. In October 2019 SoftBank agreed a rescue package that was reported to value the company at a small fraction of the January figure. WeWork later became public through a merger with a listed shell company in 2021, and filed for bankruptcy protection in the United States in November 2023.

Step 2: Key decisions

Three decisions matter. The first was the business model: sign long leases, often running many years, and fill the space with members who could leave on short notice. The second was to grow as fast as capital allowed, opening locations ahead of proven demand. The third was the decision to go public, which required a disclosure document. That disclosure is what let outsiders reverse engineer the valuation.

Step 3: Assumptions

For the private valuation to hold, several things had to be true at once. Occupancy had to stay high in every location, including new ones. Members had to keep paying prices well above the rent WeWork paid its landlords. Operating costs per desk had to fall as the company grew. And investors had to accept that this was a technology business, valued on growth, rather than a real estate business, valued on cash flow and risk. When analysts read the filing, they ran exactly the exercise from yesterday's lesson. They took the reported revenue, the reported losses and the reported lease commitments, and asked what occupancy and margin would justify the price. The answers required things the reported history did not show.

Say that out loud now.

Step 4: Incentives

Roman's view from the lender's chair: follow who is paid for what. Private investors had marked their holdings at the last funding price, so a lower public price would show a loss on their books. The founder held shares with extra voting power, which meant outside shareholders could not easily overrule him. The filing also disclosed related-party dealings, including leases on buildings in which the founder had an interest and a payment for the rights to the word "We," which was later reported to have been returned. None of that proves bad faith. It does show a structure where the people setting the price were not the people who would bear the risk if it was wrong.

Step 5: Warning signs ignored

The mismatch was visible long before the filing. A tenant that owes rent for many years and collects from members who can leave in a month carries the full risk of a downturn with almost none of the protection. Losses grew alongside revenue rather than shrinking as the company scaled, which is the opposite of what the growth story claimed. Governance gave one person unusual control. Each of these was a sign; together they described a real estate company being priced as if it were not one.

Step 6: Point of no return

For the public offering, the point of no return was the filing itself. Once the numbers were public, no amount of presentation could change the arithmetic, and the market's reverse calculation became the price. For the business, the deeper point of no return came earlier, when the long lease commitments were signed. Those obligations could not be reduced quickly when demand fell, which is why the later bankruptcy process centred on rejecting and renegotiating leases.

Step 7: Root cause

The root cause was a price set by a story rather than by what the underlying asset could support, sustained by private capital that did not have to do the reverse arithmetic until it was forced into public view. Underneath that sat a maturity mismatch: long fixed obligations funded by short, cancellable income.

The same test on a small deal

Hypothetical round numbers. A partner offers you a long head lease on a building: you pay the landlord $600,000 a year for 15 years, and you sublet the space in short furnished leases. His projection shows $1,000,000 a year of income at 90 percent occupancy, with $250,000 of operating costs, so $150,000 of profit a year.

Reverse it. Split the costs. The rent of $600,000 is fixed. Suppose $150,000 of the operating costs are also fixed, such as insurance and staff, and $100,000 are variable, such as cleaning and utilities, which move with occupancy. Full income at 100 percent occupancy is $1,000,000 divided by 0.9, about $1,111,000, and the variable costs at full occupancy are about $111,000, so each percentage point of occupancy is worth about $10,000 a year after its variable cost. The fixed load is $750,000. Breakeven occupancy is $750,000 divided by $10,000 per point, which is 75 percent. So the whole profit lives in the band between 75 and 90 percent occupancy. At 60 percent occupancy you lose $150,000 a year. Over 15 years you will see at least one downturn, and short leases empty quickly. Total rent owed is 15 years times $600,000, or $9,000,000, against $150,000 a year of hoped-for margin. That is the WeWork shape at kitchen-table scale.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is paying for a narrative because the arithmetic is uncomfortable. The control is Rule 17, applied without exception: reverse every price into the rent, occupancy, cost and return it requires, test each against evidence, and if the public numbers cannot make the price work, decline. A second control from Roman: never sign a long fixed obligation against short income without knowing the breakeven occupancy and how long your reserves last below it.

The beginner's mistake

Assuming that a high price paid by sophisticated investors proves the price is right. Sophisticated investors can be anchored to their own last price, and private markets do not force anyone to do the arithmetic. The market only tested this price when the numbers became public. Do the test yourself, earlier, while it is still cheap.

Rule 17

Before I pay or accept any price, I reverse it into the rent, occupancy, cost and return it requires, and I test each against evidence; if the public numbers cannot make the price work, I do not pay for the story.

Callback

In the second pro forma week, Sage taught lease-up and absorption: the pace at which the market actually takes up space. WeWork's model assumed every new location would fill fast and stay full. Absorption is the number that tests that assumption, and in the small example above it is the band between breakeven and projected occupancy that decides whether you make money at all.

Recap

A very large private valuation fell apart once a public filing let outsiders reverse engineer it. The flaws were a long-lease, short-income mismatch, losses that grew with scale, and governance that separated the people setting the price from the people bearing the risk. Rule 17 is the prevention: reverse every price before you pay it.

Next: JAX, on what the other side of a deal must be earning, and how to read their money from the outside.
checklist: Reverse every price into the rent, occupancy, cost and return it requires.
Identify every long fixed obligation and the income that pays it.
Calculate breakeven occupancy before signing any lease or head lease.
Measure how many months your reserves last below breakeven.
Read related-party dealings and voting control before trusting a valuation.
Ask whether losses shrink or grow as the business scales.
Never treat a price paid by sophisticated investors as proof of value.
head: Field checklist
speak: In 2019 WeWork filed to go public after a private round that was widely reported to value it near 47 billion dollars. The filing let outsiders do the arithmetic. Underneath the branding it was a real estate business: long leases to landlords, short cancellable memberships from members. Losses grew with revenue instead of shrinking, and governance gave the founder unusual control, including related-party dealings. Analysts reversed the reported numbers into the occupancy and margins the price required, and the numbers did not support the story. The offering was pulled, the founder stepped down, and a rescue came at a fraction of the earlier price. The root cause was a price set by narrative, protected from the reverse arithmetic by private capital, sitting on a maturity mismatch. My rule: before I pay or accept any price, I reverse it into what it requires and test each line against evidence. If the public numbers cannot make it work, I do not pay for the story.
terms: Maturity mismatch — funding long, fixed obligations with income that can stop or leave on short notice.
Related-party transaction — a deal between a company and someone who controls or influences it, such as a founder or director.
Breakeven occupancy — the occupancy at which income just covers every fixed obligation and operating cost.

hostile.q: Your projection shows a profitable head lease. What occupancy do you need just to pay the landlord, and how long can you survive below it?
hostile.a: Breakeven is 75 percent on our assumptions, against 90 percent projected, so the whole margin sits in a 15-point band. Each point of occupancy is worth about 10,000 dollars a year, so at 60 percent we lose 150,000 a year; our reserve covers two years of that. Because a 15-year lease will see a downturn, we will only sign with a break option or a cap on our liability, and I will not sign the lease on the projection alone.

title: Reading the other side's money from the outside
summary: A negotiation goes better when you know roughly what the other side has paid, what they owe and what return they need. Much of that can be worked out from public records and a few honest assumptions. This lesson reverse engineers a seller's floor and a buyer's levered return, then turns both into negotiating limits.
body:
Mr Shabazz, the person across the table has a number they cannot go below, and it is usually visible from the outside if you know where to look. Reverse engineering their money tells you where the deal can land before anyone names a price.

Recall

Q. From the valuation week: what is the difference between as-is and as-complete value?

A. As-is is the value in today's physical and legal condition. As-complete assumes, as a hypothetical condition, that the planned building is finished and leased. Quote the condition whenever you quote the second.

Q. From the returns week: what is cash-on-cash return?

A. One year's cash distributed to the equity holders divided by the equity they invested. It ignores timing and the sale, so it is a snapshot, not a return over the life of the deal.

Q. From the first phase: what is anchoring?

A. The tendency for the first number mentioned to pull every later estimate toward it, even when everyone knows it was arbitrary.

Why this matters

Most negotiators guess what the other side needs. A developer who can estimate it walks in with two numbers in his pocket: his own walk-away price and the other side's likely floor. The gap between them is the zone where a deal is possible. If there is no gap, you save months. If there is a gap, you know how much room you have and you are far less likely to be anchored by an opening ask.

The seller's floor

Plain English: a seller will not accept less than whatever lets them pay their debts and feel they have not lost. Some of that is arithmetic and some is psychology, and both can be estimated.

The professional framing has three public clues. The first is the seller's purchase price and date, often visible in the land registry or in a transfer tax record. The second is registered debt: a mortgage or charge on title shows a lender's claim and sometimes its amount. The third is time on market and any price reductions, visible in listing histories.

Worked example one, hypothetical round numbers. The registry shows the seller bought the land 10 years ago for $1,000,000. It is listed at $3,000,000. A mortgage of $2,000,000 is registered against it. Your own residual analysis says the land carries about $2,400,000.

First, the seller's history. Growing from $1,000,000 to $3,000,000 over 10 years is a compound rate of about 11.6 percent a year. At your $2,400,000 the seller still gets 2.4 times their money, about 9.1 percent a year. That is a story you can tell honestly: "You have done well on this land even at our price."

Second, the floor. The registered mortgage means the seller probably needs at least $2,000,000 to clear the debt, plus selling costs and any tax on the gain. If selling costs and tax are, say, $250,000 in total, which you must not assume without advice on their actual position, the hard floor is about $2,250,000. Your $2,400,000 sits $150,000 above it. The zone of possible agreement is between about $2,250,000 and $2,400,000. You now know not to open far below the floor, because a seller who cannot repay their lender cannot sell to you at any price.

Say that out loud now.

The buyer's return

The same reading works on a competitor or a partner. If you know roughly what they paid and how deals are typically financed, you can estimate the return they are chasing, and therefore how much more they could pay before walking.

Worked example two, using the site from Sage's lesson. Total cost is $18,600,000, including $3,000,000 for land. Suppose construction lenders in this market typically lend 65 percent of cost, a commercial practice rather than a rule. The loan is about $12,090,000 and the equity is about $6,510,000. Finished value at a 5 percent cap rate is $23,400,000, so profit is $4,800,000. The equity gets back $6,510,000 plus $4,800,000, or $11,310,000. That is an equity multiple of about 1.74 times.

If the project takes about 3 years from purchase to sale, the levered internal rate of return (IRR) is roughly the cube root of 1.74, less one, which is about 20 percent a year. This shortcut treats all equity as going in at the start and all money coming out at the end, so it is a rough check, not a model. Now stress it. If the finished building sells for 5 percent less, value is $22,230,000, profit falls to $3,630,000, the multiple falls to about 1.56 and the rough IRR to about 16 percent. A 5 percent fall in value removed about a quarter of the profit. That is leverage, and it tells you how little room the buyer had above $3,000,000.

Turning both readings into limits

Write three numbers before any meeting. Your walk-away price, from your own residual. The other side's estimated floor or ceiling, from the reverse reading. And the evidence grade behind the estimate. Then decide your opening position inside the zone, not outside it. An opening far outside the zone does not anchor a well-advised counterpart; it tells them you have not done the work.

Wealth Ledger

Warrick's note: run the same reverse reading on your own balance sheet. For every asset, write down what you paid, what you owe against it, and what you could sell it for after costs and tax. The gap between the last two is your true equity, and dividing your annual income from the asset by that true equity gives the return your money is actually earning today, which is often lower than the return you remember. That is a reason to review, not a reason to act; a licensed adviser is required before you act.

Monthly thread: ethics in gathering information

Public information is fair to use: registries, filings, listings, published reports and what people choose to tell you. What is not fair is any attempt to obtain what someone has a duty to keep private: asking an employee, lender or consultant to share confidential figures, paying for leaks, or misrepresenting who you are to get a document. Each of these can be a breach of contract or a legal wrong, and in some cases worse.

The practical test is simple. Would you be comfortable explaining, in front of the other side and a judge, exactly how you learned each number you are using? If the answer is no, do not use it, and say so to whoever offered it. Your reputation for clean dealing is an asset that compounds faster than any single deal.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is mistaking your estimate of their position for knowledge. The registry shows a mortgage amount at registration, not today's balance; the seller may have paid it down or added other debts you cannot see. The control is to treat every reverse reading as a hypothesis, test it with open questions in the meeting, such as "What timing works best for you?", and update your limits when the answers do not fit.

The beginner's mistake

Telling the other side what you have worked out about them. "I know you owe $2,000,000" feels powerful and lands as an intrusion. It hardens positions and invites them to dispute your numbers instead of negotiating. Keep the reading private and let it shape your offers silently.

Callback

In the psychology week you met loss aversion: people feel a loss more sharply than an equal gain. The seller's purchase price matters for exactly that reason. A price below what they paid feels like a loss even when it is fair today, and a price that still doubles their money feels like a win. Reading their history tells you which frame to offer.

Recap

Estimate the seller's floor from their purchase price, registered debt and listing history. Estimate a buyer's return from their price and typical financing, then stress it. Write your walk-away, their estimated limit and your evidence grade before you meet, and open inside the zone.

Next: Vera, on what the public record can and cannot tell you, and the rules on using it.
checklist: Pull the seller's purchase price and date from the registry or transfer record.
Check title for registered mortgages or charges and note the amounts.
Review the listing history: time on market and price reductions.
Estimate the seller's floor, with selling costs and tax confirmed by advice.
Estimate a competing buyer's levered return and stress it by 5 percent on value.
Write your walk-away, their estimated limit and the evidence grade before meeting.
Never use information someone had a duty to keep confidential.
head: Field checklist
speak: Before I negotiate I estimate the other side's money. For a seller, the registry often shows what they paid and when, and whether a mortgage is registered. If they bought for a million ten years ago and owe two million, their hard floor is about two million plus selling costs and tax, and I check those with advice rather than assuming. For a buyer, I take their price and typical financing and estimate their levered return. On an 18.6 million project at 65 percent loan to cost, a 4.8 million profit is about a 1.74 times equity multiple, roughly 20 percent a year over three years. A 5 percent fall in value cuts that to about 16 percent, which shows how little room they have. I write three numbers before every meeting: my walk-away, their estimated limit and the evidence grade. I open inside the zone, I keep my reading private, and I only use information I could explain to a judge.
terms: Zone of possible agreement — the range between one side's walk-away price and the other side's, where a deal can be made.
Registered charge — a lender's or other party's claim recorded against a property's title in the land registry.
Seller's basis — what the seller originally paid for the property, which shapes both their tax and how a price feels to them.

hostile.q: You have offered 2.4 million. The seller says they will not take less than 2.8 and you are wasting their time. What now?
hostile.a: I would thank them and restate the basis: at today's rents and published costs the site carries 2.4 million at the margin our lenders need, and I can show the calculation. I would ask what they see that would justify 2.8, such as density, a signed tenant or lower costs. If they show me evidence, I will rerun it. If not, I would leave an option open at 2.4 with a price uplift only if extra density is approved, and walk away without improving the base price.

title: What the public record proves, and what it only suggests
summary: Public records are the raw material of reverse engineering, but each one proves something narrower than it appears to. A registered price may not be the economic price, and many transfers never appear on title at all. This lesson grades the main records by what they prove and sets out the rules that limit how information may be gathered and used.
body:
Mr Shabazz, a public record proves exactly what it records and nothing more. A registered price proves that a number was written on a transfer, not that it was the real economic price, and the deals that matter most are sometimes the ones the registry never sees.

Recall

Q. From yesterday: what three public clues help you estimate a seller's floor?

A. Their purchase price and date, any mortgage or charge registered on title, and the listing history, including time on market and price reductions.

Q. From the returns week: what is after-tax leakage?

A. The gap between the return a pre-tax model shows and the return that reaches the owner once entity-level and personal taxes are paid.

Q. From the first phase: why keep a decision journal?

A. To record what you believed and why at the time you decided, so you can later judge the decision on its reasoning rather than on its outcome, and learn from both.

Why this matters

This week you are building conclusions from public information: implied land prices, implied rents, the other side's likely floor. Every one of those conclusions inherits the weaknesses of its sources. If you treat a registry entry as if it were an audited fact about the whole economic deal, your reverse engineering will be precise and wrong. And if you gather information the wrong way, you can expose yourself to a claim that costs more than the deal is worth.

The main records, graded

Plain English first: each kind of record answers one narrow question. Know the question and you know the limit.

The professional framing, in general terms, because the details differ from place to place and you must verify them locally.

  • The land registry or title record. Proves who holds registered title and what interests, such as mortgages and easements, have been registered. It often shows a stated price. It does not prove the terms behind that price.
  • Transfer tax or land transfer records. Where they exist and are accessible, they show the consideration declared for tax. Declared consideration is what the parties chose to state, within the rules.
  • Property assessment rolls. Show a value assigned for property tax, usually by a mass method, as of a base date. They are useful as a trend and a cross-check, and weak as a market value for one building.
  • Planning and permit files. Show what has been applied for, approved and conditioned. An application proves intent; an approval proves permission; neither proves the building will be built.
  • Corporate and securities filings. For companies that must file, these can disclose leases, debts and asset values in detail. They are often the richest source on a large owner, as the WeWork filing showed.
  • Court records. Show disputes, judgments and sometimes the documents behind them. They prove that a claim was made and how it was decided, not that every allegation was true.

When the recorded price is not the price

Worked example one, hypothetical round numbers. The registry shows a land sale at $3,000,000. You later learn the seller lent $2,000,000 of it back to the buyer, a vendor take-back mortgage, at 2 percent a year for 3 years, when a bank would have charged about 7 percent. The buyer saves 5 percent of $2,000,000, which is $100,000 a year, or about $300,000 over the 3 years before discounting. In economic terms the buyer paid closer to $2,700,000 for the land and received a cheap loan worth the difference. If you used $3,000,000 as your comparable, you overstated the land value by about 10 percent.

Other common gaps between recorded and economic price: the seller agreed to keep a unit or a parking space; the buyer assumed a liability; the price was split between land and a separate payment for plans, permits or equipment; or the parties were related and the price was not set at arm's length, meaning between independent parties each acting in their own interest.

Say that out loud now.

The deals the registry never sees

In many places a building can change hands without the title changing at all, because what is sold is the company that owns it. A share sale, or a sale of an interest in a partnership that owns the land, may leave the registered owner exactly as it was. The registry shows nothing, and the market price of that deal may only be known from a press release, a filing or a broker.

Worked example two. A site sold 3 years ago for $2,000,000 when the zoning allowed 40 apartments, which is $50,000 per buildable apartment. Since then the site was rezoned for 60 apartments. Your comparable is not $50,000 per apartment today, and it is not $2,000,000 divided by 60, which is about $33,000. It is a sale under different rules at a different date. To use it, you must adjust for the change in permitted density and for 3 years of market movement, and say plainly that both adjustments are judgements. A recorded fact used under the wrong conditions becomes a misleading one.

The rules on gathering and using information

Concepts only; the specifics depend on where you are, so verify them against the primary source before you rely on them, and get advice where it matters.

Confidentiality. Information shared under a non-disclosure agreement, or obtained by someone who owes a duty of confidence, such as an employee, lender or consultant, generally cannot be used for purposes outside that duty. Using it can expose you to a claim even if you did not sign anything yourself.

Privacy and data rules. Personal information about individuals, including owners, tenants and buyers, is commonly regulated. A public register does not automatically mean every use of the data is allowed.

Terms of use. Commercial databases and listing services usually license their data on terms that limit copying, scraping and redistribution.

Securities rules. Where a company's shares are publicly traded, using material information that has not been made public to trade, or passing it on, is commonly prohibited.

Your own statements. When you put reverse-engineered numbers into an investor memo or a lender package, they become your representations. Label each one with its source and its grade, so no reader mistakes an inference for a fact.

Professional sign-off required: a lawyer licensed where you operate, before you rely on any record for a binding decision or use any information whose source is unclear.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is laundering a guess through a record: taking a registered price, an assessment or a planning application, and repeating it as if it proved the economic fact you need. The control is a source column in every analysis, stating what each record proves and what it does not, and a rule that any comparable used in a decision is confirmed by at least two independent sources or marked as single-source.

The beginner's mistake

Assuming that a quiet registry means a quiet market. When nothing has been registered nearby for a year, the beginner concludes there is no evidence. Often the deals happened as share sales, options or unregistered agreements. Ask brokers, lenders and appraisers what traded, and record what they say as reported, not as proved.

Callback

In the valuation week REGA taught the intended user and the effective date of an appraisal: an opinion of value is only valid for the purpose, the reader and the date it was written for. Public records work the same way. Every record has a date, a purpose and a narrow scope, and using it outside those limits turns good evidence into bad.

Recap

Grade every record by what it proves. A registered price may hide vendor financing, side payments or related-party terms. Share sales and options may never appear on title. Gather information only in ways you could explain to a judge, and label every reverse-engineered number with its source when you hand it to someone else.

Next: Sage, with a full worked calculation from public inputs to an implied land price, rent and return.
checklist: Write down what each record proves and what it does not.
Ask whether a recorded price included vendor financing, side payments or assumed liabilities.
Check whether the buyer and seller were related or independent.
Adjust any older comparable for changed zoning and for time.
Ask brokers and lenders about share sales and options the registry cannot see.
Confirm any decision-critical comparable from two independent sources.
Label every reverse-engineered number in a memo with its source and grade.
head: Field checklist
speak: A public record proves exactly what it records. The land registry proves registered title and registered interests, and often shows a stated price, but not the terms behind it. If the seller lent two million back at 2 percent when banks charge 7, the buyer saved about 300,000 over three years, so a 3 million registered price was closer to 2.7 million in economic terms. Some deals never reach the registry, because the company that owns the land is sold instead. Older sales happened under older rules, so a sale at 40 permitted units must be adjusted before it is compared with a site zoned for 60. When I gather information I stay with what is public or freely given, I respect confidentiality, privacy and database terms, and I label every reverse-engineered number with its source when it goes into a memo, because at that point it becomes my representation.
terms: Vendor take-back mortgage — a loan from the seller to the buyer for part of the purchase price, which can make the recorded price higher than the economic price.
Arm's length — a transaction between independent parties each acting in their own interest, the basis for a price that reflects the market.
Share sale — selling the company or entity that owns a property rather than the property itself, so the registered owner may not change.

hostile.q: Your investor memo says land in this area trades at 75,000 per buildable unit. Where does that number come from, and would you stake your reputation on it?
hostile.a: It comes from three registered sales in the last 18 months, adjusted for density and date, which I list in the appendix with their sources. Two are confirmed by the brokers on each side; the third is single-source and marked as such. One of the three included vendor financing, which I have removed from the price. So I would stand behind it as a range of about 68,000 to 80,000, not as a single figure, and the memo says that.

title: From a zoning map and three listings to a land price
summary: This lesson builds an implied land price step by step from inputs anyone can find: site area, permitted density, listed rents, published costs and a market cap rate. It then reverses a recorded sale into the rent that sale requires. The result shows why land, as the residual, swings far more than any single input.
body:
Mr Shabazz, with a site area, a zoning map, three rental listings and a cost guide, you can estimate what a piece of land is worth before you speak to anyone. Today we do it step by step, with units, and then test a real-looking sale against it.

Recall

Q. From yesterday: why might a registered sale price overstate the economic price?

A. Because the deal may have included vendor financing at a below-market rate, a side payment, an assumed liability, or terms between related parties. The registry shows the stated number, not the terms behind it.

Q. From the returns week: what does levered mean?

A. Measured on the equity after the loan. Debt magnifies the return on equity in both directions, so a levered return is higher in good cases and falls further in bad ones.

Q. From the first phase: what is a pre-mortem?

A. Imagining the project has already failed and writing down why, before you commit, so the risks are named while they can still be changed.

Why this matters

Land is the first and largest decision you control, and it is the one most often priced by emotion. A seller's asking price and a broker's enthusiasm are not evidence. Twenty minutes with public inputs gives you an independent figure, and more importantly, it shows you which assumption the land price depends on most.

The inputs, all hypothetical

Site area: 2,000 square metres, from the registry plan. Permitted floor area ratio (FAR), meaning the total floor area allowed divided by the site area: 3.0, from the zoning by-law. Efficiency, meaning rentable area as a share of gross floor area after corridors, stairs and walls: 80 percent, a working figure. Listed rents for new apartments nearby: about $30 per square metre per month. Vacancy and credit loss: 5 percent. Operating expenses: 30 percent of collected income. Market cap rate for new apartment buildings: 5 percent. Hard costs: $2,500 per square metre of gross floor area, from a published guide. Soft costs: 18 percent of hard costs. Finance costs: 8 percent of hard and soft costs. Required developer's profit: 15 percent on total cost, which is a commercial practice in some markets, not a standard.

Step 1: From site to building

Gross floor area is 2,000 square metres times 3.0, which is 6,000 square metres. Rentable area is 80 percent of that, 4,800 square metres. At an average of 60 square metres per apartment, that is 80 apartments.

Step 2: From building to NOI

Potential gross rent is 4,800 square metres times $30 times 12 months, which is $1,728,000 a year. Less 5 percent vacancy, effective gross income is $1,641,600. Less 30 percent operating expenses, which is $492,480, net operating income (NOI) is $1,149,120 a year.

Step 3: From NOI to value

Value is $1,149,120 divided by 0.05, which is $22,982,400. Call it $23,000,000. That is the as-complete value: what the building would be worth finished and stabilised, under the assumption that it gets built as permitted.

Step 4: Costs before land

Hard costs are 6,000 square metres times $2,500, which is $15,000,000. Soft costs at 18 percent are $2,700,000. Finance costs at 8 percent of $17,700,000 are $1,416,000. In a full model finance cost also depends on the land price, which creates a small loop; we ignore it here to keep the steps clear. Non-land cost is $19,116,000.

Step 5: Solve for the land

A 15 percent profit on cost means value equals total cost times 1.15. So total cost allowed is $22,982,400 divided by 1.15, about $19,984,700. Subtract the $19,116,000 of non-land cost. The land can carry about $868,700, roughly $870,000. That is about $10,900 per apartment, or about $145 per buildable square metre of gross floor area.

Say that out loud now.

Worked example two: test a recorded sale

The registry shows a similar site nearby sold last year for $1,500,000. Do not conclude that you are wrong or that the buyer is foolish. Reverse it.

With land at $1,500,000, total cost is $20,616,000. For a 15 percent profit, value must be $20,616,000 times 1.15, which is $23,708,400. At a 5 percent cap rate, that needs NOI of $1,185,420. Working back up the staircase: effective gross income is NOI divided by 0.70, about $1,693,500. Potential gross rent is that divided by 0.95, about $1,782,600. Divide by 4,800 square metres and 12 months: about $30.95 per square metre per month.

So the $1,500,000 price needs rents about 3 percent above today's listings, with everything else the same. That is close. Yet the land price is 72 percent higher than your residual. How can a 3 percent difference in rent produce a 72 percent difference in land?

Why the land swings so hard

Because land is the residual. Every other claim, construction, fees, interest and profit, is fixed or scales with cost, and only the land absorbs a change in value. Measure it. One extra dollar per square metre per month is $57,600 a year of potential rent. After vacancy and expenses that is 57,600 times 0.95 times 0.70, about $38,300 of NOI. At a 5 percent cap rate that is about $766,000 of value. After the 15 percent profit, about $666,000 more that the land can carry.

So a rent change of about 3 percent moves the land price by about $666,000, which is roughly 77 percent of the $870,000 residual. The same leverage works on costs: a 5 percent increase in hard costs, $750,000, plus the soft and finance costs that follow it, wipes out the whole residual. This is why two careful people can value the same land very differently, and why you should never quote a residual without its sensitivity.

Reading the result

Write the conclusion as a range and a list. "Land carries roughly $500,000 to $1,500,000, depending mainly on rent. At $1,500,000, the deal requires rents of about $31 per square metre per month and hard costs at or below $2,500. Yield on cost at that price would be $1,149,120 divided by $20,616,000, about 5.6 percent, a spread of only about 60 basis points over the cap rate at today's rents." That last line is what a lender will see first, so it is the line to test hardest.

Then decide what to buy before you buy the land. The rent is the input that moves the answer most, so a rent survey of the newest competing buildings, with concessions and actual signed rents rather than asking rents, is worth more than any other study at this stage. The floor area is second, so a quick massing study by an architect comes next. Only after both would you spend on geotechnical or environmental work. Reverse engineering does not replace diligence; it tells you which diligence to buy first.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is quoting the middle of a residual as if it were the value. Because land is leveraged to every other input, the middle is the least informative number on the page. The control is a one-line sensitivity on every residual you write: the change in land value for a one-dollar move in rent per square metre and for a 5 percent move in hard costs.

The beginner's mistake

Using the maximum permitted density as if it were guaranteed. The by-law permits a floor area ratio of 3.0, but setbacks, height limits, parking and fire access may stop you reaching it on this site. Check what the envelope actually fits before you multiply by it. Professional sign-off required: an architect or planner, to confirm the achievable area.

Callback

In the second pro forma week Sage built the income staircase: potential gross rent, less vacancy, to effective gross income, less expenses, to NOI. Today you climbed that staircase in both directions, down to a value and back up from a required value to a required rent. The same staircase, read backward, is how you test every price you are shown.

Recap

Site area times floor area ratio gives the building, rents give NOI, the cap rate gives value, and value less non-land cost and profit gives the land. Reverse any recorded sale into the rent it needs, and always show how hard the land moves for a small change in rent or cost.

Next: Remi, in the room with a broker who wants an offer on the spot.
checklist: Confirm site area from the registry plan and floor area ratio from the by-law.
Apply an efficiency factor before turning floor area into rentable area.
Build NOI with vacancy and operating expenses, never from gross rent.
Separate non-land cost into hard, soft and finance before solving for land.
Reverse every recorded sale into the rent it requires.
Report land value as a range with a one-line sensitivity.
Have an architect or planner confirm the achievable floor area.
head: Field checklist
speak: Here is how I price land from public inputs. Site area times floor area ratio gives gross floor area: 2,000 square metres at 3.0 is 6,000. At 80 percent efficiency that is 4,800 rentable square metres. At 30 dollars a square metre a month, less 5 percent vacancy and 30 percent expenses, NOI is about 1.15 million. At a 5 percent cap rate the finished building is worth about 23 million. Non-land costs are about 19.1 million. With a 15 percent profit on cost, the land carries about 870,000. A nearby site sold for 1.5 million, which needs rents only about 3 percent higher. That small rent gap explains a large land gap because land is the residual: one dollar more rent per square metre moves the land by about 666,000. So I never quote a residual without its sensitivity, and I confirm the achievable floor area with an architect.
terms: Floor area ratio — total permitted floor area divided by site area, used by zoning to control density.
Efficiency — rentable or saleable area as a share of gross floor area after corridors, stairs and walls.
Residual land value — the finished value less all non-land costs and the required profit, which is what the land can carry.

hostile.q: Your residual says 870,000, the seller wants 1.5 million, and you say they could both be reasonable. That sounds like a model that tells me nothing. Which is it?
hostile.a: It tells you exactly where the disagreement lives. The two prices differ by about 3 percent in rent and nothing else. So the decision is not a modelling question; it is whether achievable rent here is 30 dollars a square metre or 31. I have commissioned a rent survey of the four newest buildings. If it supports 31, I will pay close to 1.5 million. If it supports 30, I will offer under a million or walk.

title: The broker who wants an offer before you leave
summary: A broker presents a site with an asking price, a story and a deadline. This lesson scripts the meeting: how to reverse the price aloud without arguing, what never to say, what the broker is really asking, and when silence earns more than speech. The goal is to leave with information and a relationship, not a rushed offer.
body:
Mr Shabazz, a broker who asks for an offer on the spot is usually asking for an anchor, not a deal. Your job in that room is to turn the asking price into the assumptions it requires, out loud and without hostility, and to leave with information rather than a commitment.

Recall

Q. From yesterday: why does a small change in rent move the land price so much?

A. Because land is the residual. Construction, fees, interest and profit are fixed or scale with cost, so the whole change in value lands on the land.

Q. From the valuation week: what is an extraordinary assumption?

A. An uncertain fact assumed true on the valuation date that would change the value if false, such as a pending rezoning. Quote it in the same sentence as the value.

Q. From the communication weeks: what are the three steps for a hostile question?

A. Acknowledge the concern, bridge to what you know, then answer with a fact or a commitment, such as "I'll confirm by Friday."

Why this matters

Brokers are the main channel through which land reaches a small developer. A good broker relationship brings you sites before they are widely marketed. A bad first meeting brands you as either a soft touch or a time-waster. The meeting is also where anchoring happens: the asking price is the first number spoken, and if you react to it emotionally, it shapes every number that follows.

The scene

This is a composite scene with hypothetical numbers. Dana, a commercial broker you have met once, has invited you to view a 2,000 square metre site. The asking price is $1,800,000. She says the zoning allows a floor area ratio of 3.0, rents nearby are "about $32 a square metre," and two other developers are "circling." She would like a letter of intent by Friday. You did the residual on the drive over and got roughly $870,000 at $30 rents, and about $1,500,000 if rents reach $31.

The question behind the question

When Dana says "two other developers are circling," the question behind it is "How much do you want this?" She is testing urgency. When she asks "What would it take for you to make an offer?", the question behind it is "Give me a number I can take back to the seller." Her fee usually depends on a sale closing, and often on its price, so her incentive is speed and a high anchor. That is not a criticism; it is her job. Yours is different.

The lines to say

Open with interest and process, not price: "Thanks, Dana. This is the kind of site I want. Let me tell you how I'll get to a number, so you know I'm serious."

Reverse the price out loud, as a question, not an accusation: "At $1,800,000, by my rough numbers the building needs rents nearer $31.50 a square metre than $30, with costs where the guides put them. Are you seeing signed rents at that level, or asking rents?"

Ask for the evidence you need: "Could you send me the registry plan, any planning history, and the last three land sales you'd use as comparables? I'll come back with a view by Friday." That is the bridge to "I'll confirm by Friday" from the communication weeks, and it gives her something to report to the seller.

Name your process: "I'll make an offer once I've checked the rent and the achievable floor area. If the numbers work, I move quickly."

Say that out loud now.

Worked example: the arithmetic you do aloud

You will not have a spreadsheet in the room, so carry two shortcuts. The first: on this site, each dollar per square metre per month of rent moves the land by about $666,000, from Sage's sensitivity. The asking price is about $930,000 above your $30-rent residual. Divide $930,000 by $666,000 and you get about 1.4. So the asking price needs rents about $1.40 higher, roughly $31.40, which you can round aloud to "about $31.50."

The second shortcut is cost. A 5 percent rise in hard costs, with the soft and finance costs that follow it, removes about $950,000 of land value. If Dana says "costs are coming down," you can answer: "That would help. Every 5 percent on hard costs is worth about $950,000 of land here, so I'll want a contractor's view before I count on it."

Two shortcuts, prepared in advance, let you respond to any claim in her pitch with a number rather than a feeling. That is what makes a broker take you seriously.

The lines never to say

Never say "That's way too high." It is an opinion with no evidence and it invites her to defend the price. Never say a number you have not decided: "Would they take a million?" becomes the floor of your negotiation and a rumour in the market. Never say "I need to run it past my partners" if you have no partners; she will learn, and your credibility will go with it. Never criticise the seller. And never say "I'll beat any other offer," which hands the other buyers your money.

When to stay silent

Stay silent immediately after she names the price. A pause of three or four seconds, while you look at the site plan, signals that you are thinking, not reacting. Stay silent after you ask whether the rents are signed or asking; let her answer fully, because the way she answers is information. And stay silent about your residual. If she asks "What's your number?", the answer is "I'll have one by Friday, with the reasons."

A second exchange

Dana pushes: "If you wait until Friday you might lose it." Acknowledge, bridge, answer: "I understand, and if someone else is sure enough to commit today, they may be the right buyer. I'd rather give you a number I'll close at than one I'll retrade later. Friday, with my reasoning." Retrading, meaning lowering an agreed price after diligence, is the fastest way to lose a broker's trust, and saying you will not do it is worth more than speed.

Holding your state

Your body will tell you when the pressure lands: a quicker pulse, an urge to fill silence, a pull toward agreeing. Slow your speech slightly and lower your voice at the end of sentences, which reads as settled rather than uncertain. Breathe out fully before you answer a pressing question; a longer exhale tends to calm the stress response, a practitioner habit with research behind it, and one to do while standing still, never while driving. Remind yourself of the gate: no offer leaves without the rent and the floor area checked. The rule decides, not the mood of the room.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is being anchored into an offer by urgency. The control is a standing rule that you never put a number in writing in the first meeting on a new site, combined with a firm, short deadline you set yourself, so you are not slow, only disciplined.

The beginner's mistake

Treating the broker as an opponent. She represents the seller, but she also decides which buyers hear about the next site. Be clear, quick, honest and consistent, and you become the buyer she calls first. Win the relationship even when you lose the site.

Callback

In the psychology week you learned anchoring and loss aversion. The asking price is the anchor, and "two other developers are circling" is an appeal to loss aversion: the fear of missing out. Naming both silently to yourself in the room weakens their hold. Reversing the anchor into rent turns it from a number you react to into a claim you test.

Recap

Open with interest and process. Reverse the asking price aloud into the rent it requires. Ask for the evidence, set your own short deadline and keep your residual to yourself. Carry two prepared shortcuts so every claim gets a number, not a feeling.

Next: Kema, with the week's six questions, a Red Pen drill and the boardroom drill.
checklist: Run the residual and two sensitivities before the meeting.
Open with interest and process, never with a reaction to price.
Reverse the asking price aloud into the rent it requires.
Ask whether rents are signed or only asked.
Request the registry plan, planning history and three comparables.
Set your own short deadline and never write a number in the first meeting.
Keep your residual private until you are ready to offer.
head: Field checklist
speak: When a broker asks for an offer on the spot, she is asking for an anchor. I open with interest and process: this is the kind of site I want, and here is how I will get to a number. Then I reverse the asking price aloud as a question. On this site each dollar of rent per square metre is worth about 666,000 of land, so an asking price 930,000 above my residual needs rents about a dollar forty higher. I ask whether she is seeing signed rents at that level or asking rents. I ask for the registry plan, the planning history and three comparables, and I set my own deadline: a view by Friday, with reasons. I never say a number I have not decided, never call the price too high, and never promise to beat other offers. I stay silent after she names the price, and I keep my residual private.
terms: Anchor — the first number put on the table, which pulls later estimates toward it.
Retrading — lowering an agreed price after diligence, which damages trust with brokers and sellers.
Signed rent — the rent actually agreed in a lease, as opposed to the asking rent advertised.

hostile.q: Two other groups are ready to sign a letter of intent today at the asking price. Why should the seller wait for you?
hostile.a: They should not, if those offers are firm and will close at that price. I would rather lose the site than offer a number I would have to retrade. What I can offer is a decision by Friday, based on signed rents and the achievable floor area, and a buyer who closes at the number he gives. If the other offers fall away in diligence, I will still be here, with my number.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Reverse engineering a deal: quiz, Red Pen and boardroom
summary: Six questions test the week: the deal equation, the list of what must be true, reading the other side's money, the limits of public records, the residual and its sensitivity, and Rule 17. A Red Pen drill hides seven defects in a short land memo. The boardroom drill asks for the week in two minutes.
body:
Mr Shabazz, this week taught one habit: take any number you are shown and work out what must be true for it to make sense. Today we check that the habit works when you are tired and someone is pushing.

Recall

Q. From the valuation week: what is reconciliation in an appraisal?

A. The step where the appraiser weighs the income, sales comparison and cost approaches by the strength of their evidence. It is not an average.

Q. From the returns week: why read IRR beside the equity multiple?

A. Because IRR measures speed and the multiple measures amount. A high IRR on a small, quick deal can create less wealth than a lower IRR on a larger one.

Q. From the first phase: what is your liquidity floor?

A. The amount of readily available cash you will not go below, so that no single setback forces you to sell or borrow on bad terms.

Why this matters

Reverse engineering is the skill you will use most often and practise least. Lenders, brokers, partners and sellers will hand you finished numbers every week. If you can take them apart in a few minutes, you negotiate from evidence; if not, you negotiate from hope.

The six questions

Question 1. Write the deal equation in words.

Answer: Value equals stabilised net operating income divided by the market cap rate. Total cost equals land plus hard, soft and finance costs. Yield on cost equals NOI divided by total cost, and the development spread is yield on cost minus the cap rate. Fix any three of the main inputs and the fourth follows.

Question 2. What is the output of a reverse calculation?

Answer: A short list headed "What must be true," each line graded by its evidence, with the answer stated as a range. The weakest line with the biggest effect is where your diligence money goes first.

Question 3. A seller bought for $1,000,000 ten years ago and has a $2,000,000 mortgage registered. What does that suggest about their floor?

Answer: They probably need at least enough to clear the mortgage plus selling costs and any tax on the gain, so roughly $2,000,000 plus those amounts, confirmed by advice rather than assumed. A registered amount is the figure at registration, not necessarily today's balance.

Question 4. Name two ways a registered price can differ from the economic price.

Answer: Vendor financing at a below-market rate, and side payments or assumed liabilities. Related-party terms are a third. Share sales may not appear on title at all.

Question 5. On a site where each dollar per square metre per month of rent moves the land by $666,000, an asking price is $930,000 above your residual. What rent does the price imply?

Answer: About $1.40 above the rent in your residual. At $30 in the residual, the price implies roughly $31.40.

Question 6. What is Rule 17?

Answer: Before I pay or accept any price, I reverse it into the rent, occupancy, cost and return it requires, and I test each against evidence; if the public numbers cannot make the price work, I do not pay for the story.

Say that out loud now.

Recap of the week

Sage set out the one equation and the list of what must be true. Ford and Roman showed, through WeWork in 2019, how a public filing let outsiders reverse engineer a large valuation and how a long-lease, short-income mismatch sat underneath it. JAX read the other side's money: a seller's floor from registry clues and a buyer's levered return. Vera graded public records by what they prove and set out the rules on gathering information. Sage built a land price from a zoning map and listings and showed why land swings hardest. Remi took you into a broker's meeting and showed how to reverse an asking price aloud.

Red Pen drill

Here is a hypothetical one-paragraph memo a junior analyst might hand you. Read it as if you will sign it. Find the defects before you read the list.

"Land recommendation. The site is 2,000 square metres zoned at a floor area ratio of 3.0, so we will build 6,000 square metres of rentable apartments. Rents are $32 per square metre per month, based on current listings. NOI is $2,304,000 (6,000 times $32 times 12). At a 5 percent cap rate the building is worth $46,000,000. Costs are about $19,000,000, so the land is worth up to $27,000,000 and the asking price of $1,800,000 is a bargain. The registry shows the last nearby sale at $1,500,000, which confirms market value. We should offer today."

Now compare with the defects.

  1. Gross floor area is treated as rentable area. No efficiency factor was applied; at 80 percent, rentable area is 4,800 square metres, not 6,000.
  2. Asking rents from listings are treated as achieved rents, with no signed-lease evidence.
  3. The NOI is gross rent. There is no vacancy and no operating expense. It is income, not net operating income.
  4. The value inherits all three errors, so it is roughly double a realistic figure.
  5. No developer's profit is deducted before solving for land, so the "land is worth" figure is the whole margin, not a residual.
  6. A single registered sale is used as proof of market value, with no check of its terms, its date or whether it was at arm's length.
  7. "We should offer today" breaks the gate: no rent survey, no achievable-area check, no range and no sensitivity.

A senior reader would also notice what is missing entirely: the stress case. A memo that calls something a bargain should say what would make it not one.

Boardroom drill

Stand up, set a two-minute timer, and explain this week to a board that has never heard the word residual. Then compare with the model answer.

Model answer: "Every price we are shown carries assumptions inside it, and we can usually work them out from public information. A building is worth its net operating income divided by the market cap rate. It costs land, construction, fees and interest. The gap is the developer's margin. If we know the price someone paid and the public facts, zoning, rents and costs, we can solve for the rent or the return they must be expecting. We write that as a short list of what must be true, and grade each item by how good its evidence is. Land is the most sensitive number, because it absorbs every change; on a typical site, a 3 percent change in rent can move the land value by most of its total. So we never quote a land value without its sensitivity, we test the weakest assumption first, and we never pay a price we cannot reverse into believable rents and costs. That is our Rule 17."

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is doing the arithmetic and skipping the grading. A neat reverse calculation built on asking rents and gross floor area is still wrong. The control is to write the evidence grade beside every input, every time.

The beginner's mistake

Practising only on your own deals. Reverse engineer three deals a week that you are not buying: a reported land sale, a building sale, a listing. Speed comes from repetition, and the first two steps should happen in your head before the broker finishes talking.

Callback

In the communication weeks you learned to put the bottom line first. A good reverse calculation ends in one sentence you can lead with: "At this price the deal needs rents about 3 percent above today's." Everything else in the memo is support for that sentence.

Recap

One equation, one list of what must be true, one grading of evidence, one sensitivity, and Rule 17. Answer the six questions aloud once more and practise the boardroom drill before you close the app.

head: The six questions
speak: This week was one habit: take any number and work out what must be true for it to make sense. Value is net operating income over the cap rate; cost is land plus hard, soft and finance; yield on cost is NOI over cost. Fix three inputs and the fourth follows. I write the answer as a list of what must be true, grade each line by its evidence and state a range. WeWork showed what happens when a valuation meets public arithmetic: long leases funded by short memberships did not support the price. I read the other side's money from registry clues, and I remember that a registered price can hide vendor financing or side payments. Land is the residual, so it swings hardest: a 3 percent change in rent can move most of it. Rule 17: before I pay or accept a price, I reverse it and test each assumption. If the public numbers cannot make it work, I do not pay for the story.
terms: Development spread — yield on cost minus the market cap rate, the margin paid for taking development risk.
Sensitivity — how much an output changes for a stated change in one input, such as land value per dollar of rent.
Evidence grade — a label for how reliable an input is, from recorded fact to published opinion to inference.

hostile.q: Your memo calls this land a bargain at 1.8 million. What single assumption, if wrong, makes it a loss?
hostile.a: Rent. The price needs achieved rents of about 31.40 dollars a square metre a month; at today's 30 dollars the land carries about 870,000. Each dollar of rent is worth about 666,000 of land, so if signed rents come in at 30, we would be paying roughly 930,000 more than the site supports. That is why the offer is conditional on a rent survey of signed leases, and why I will not sign until it is back.
